item.title: Govt tightens terms for extending contracts of 7 pre-NELP oil, gas blocks
item.description: Under revised policy, extensions can be granted in one or more instalments of up to 30 years each, for both oil and gas fields, subject to their continued commercial viability ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: The government has revised its policy for extending production-sharing contracts (PSCs) for seven pre-New Exploration Licensing Policy (Pre-NELP) oil and gas blocks, allowing extensions until the end of a field's economic life while stipulating higher government profit shares, minimum performance requirements and investment commitments.Under the revised policy, notified by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas on November 10, extensions can be granted in one or more instalments of up to 30 years each, for both oil and gas fields, subject to their continued commercial viability.The government will receive a higher share of profit petroleum during the extended contract period, with its share set at 10 percentage points above the rate calculated under normal PSC provisions for the first 10 years of extension, five percentage points higher for the next 10 years and 2.5 percentage points higher for the following 10 years. Thereafter, the normal PSC provisions will apply.The revised policy supersedes the framework issued in April 2017 and follows the notification of the Oilfields (Regulation and Development) Amendment Act, 2025, and the Petroleum and Natural Gas Rules, 2025.The seven blocks covered by the policy are : RJ-ON-90/1 and SGL (RJ-ON/6) in Rajasthan; Dirok AAP-ON-94/1 and AA-ONJ/2 in Assam and Assam-Mizoram; and Tarapur (CB-ON/2), Palej-Pramoda (CB-ON/7) and CB-ON/3 in Gujarat.Under the new framework, contractors can apply for an extension after completing half the original contract term or its extended term, but must submit their applications at least two years before the contract expires.The Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) will make its recommendation within six months of receiving an application, while the government will decide within three months of receiving the DGH proposal.To qualify, contractors must demonstrate the availability of remaining recoverable reserves through a third-party reserves audit and submit a field development plan or revised field development plan covering the proposed extension period.The plan must include estimates of remaining reserves, future production profiles based on reservoir simulation studies, proposed work programmes and estimated expenditure, according to the notification.For development areas with remaining recoverable 2P/P50 reserves exceeding 5 million barrels of oil equivalent, the reserves audit must be conducted by an internationally reputed consultant from a panel maintained by the DGH.Contractors must also demonstrate satisfactory past performance. They should have either drilled at least 70 per cent of the development wells specified in the approved field development plan over the preceding 10 years or achieved at least 70 per cent of committed production under the approved field operating plan or work programme during the same period.They must also have cleared all statutory dues payable to the government, demonstrate technical expertise and comply with site restoration fund and site restoration plan requirements.The policy requires contractors to furnish a bank guarantee equivalent to 10 per cent of the total estimated annual expenditure under the work programme approved by the Management Committee. A grace period of up to one year may be allowed for completing delayed work, subject to an extension of the bank guarantee and other conditions.During the extended period, royalties and cess will be payable at prevailing rates applicable under the nomination regime, with contractors contributing in proportion to their participating interests.The government has retained the option to invite fresh bids if contractors fail to meet the prescribed eligibility and performance conditions. It can also assign fields to national oil companies, including Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd (OIL).The government has reserved the right to refuse an extension without assigning reasons and to impose additional conditions specific to individual contracts. Contractors unwilling to accept the revised policy will have their fields considered for rebidding on an as-is-where-is basis.The revised framework also provides that contractors can choose the seat of arbitration in accordance with Rule 51 of the Petroleum and Natural Gas Rules, 2025.Existing extensions granted under the 2017 policy will remain valid until their scheduled expiry under the terms already approved. However, all first-time extension applications beyond the original PSC term, as well as applications for further extensions beyond currently approved periods, will be governed by the revised policy.

item.title: Oil, gas import bill up 60% in Oct as Brent surges, LPG use declines
item.description: Direct private LPG imports fell 83.8 per cent in October and 97.3 per cent in April-October. Packed domestic LPG sales by state-run companies fell 11.8 per cent in October, and bulk LPG sales fell ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: India's net oil and gas import bill rose 60 per cent year-on-year to $16 billion in October as Brent crude averaged $124.77 a barrel, almost double that of a year earlier, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), part of the oil ministry.The net bill was $10.0 billion in October 2025. Crude imports alone cost $19.5 billion, against $10.4 billion a year ago, even though volumes rose only 11 per cent to 23.3 million tonnes. LNG imports cost $1.3 billion, and petroleum product exports brought in $6.3 billion.Brent averaged $116.77 in September and $64.75 in October 2025. The Indian basket averaged $119.91 in October, against $65.08 a year earlier.Over April-October, the net import bill reached $97.7 billion, up from $70.3 billion a year earlier. Crude imports rose 2.7 per cent in volume but cost $111.0 billion, against $72.3 billion.Consumption of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) fell 12.3 per cent in October and 15.1 per cent in April-October. The number of active domestic LPG customers stood at 32.6 crore on November 1, down from 33.4 crore on April 1, the PPAC data showed.Direct private LPG imports fell 83.8 per cent in October and 97.3 per cent in April-October. Packed domestic LPG sales by state-run companies fell 11.8 per cent in October, and bulk LPG sales fell 49.1 per cent. Auto LPG sales rose 23.9 per cent.Imports of petroleum products fell 41.2 per cent in October and 49.3 per cent in the fiscal year so far. PPAC attributed the fiscal-year decline mainly to lower imports of LPG, pet coke and fuel oil.The International Energy Agency said in its World Energy Outlook 2026 that LPG imports fell by over 50 per cent in the first two months of shipping disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.Other fuels held up better. Diesel consumption rose 12 per cent in October to 8.5 million tonnes, petrol rose 3.5 per cent, and bitumen rose 16.5 per cent. Total petroleum product consumption rose 2.7 per cent to 20.5 million tonnes in October. It was still down 3.2 per cent in April-October at 134.2 million tonnes.Natural gas consumption fell 7.27 per cent to 5,707 million standard cubic metres in October. LNG imports fell 6.94 per cent to 3,014 million standard cubic metres.India processed 24.1 million tonnes of crude in October, up 7.1 per cent, or about 5.70 million barrels a day. Of that, 22.0 million tonnes were imported crude, and domestic output was 2.1 million tonnes. Imports met 88.7 per cent of crude consumption in October.Domestic crude and condensate output was 2.3 million tonnes. Import dependency for natural gas stood at 52.8 per cent in October.Ethanol blending in petrol stood at 20 per cent in October, PPAC data showed.

item.description: The company is looking to expand its reach beyond established leisure destinations such as Goa and hill stations, with growing interest in cultural, spiritual, nature-led and rural tourism ...

Airbnb looks beyond traditional holiday hubs to deepen presence in India The company is looking to expand its reach beyond established leisure destinations such as Goa and hill stations, with growing interest in cultural, spiritual, nature-led and rural tourism

Technology-led initiatives are another part of the strategy, with the company introducing AI-powered tools for searching, filtering and comparing homes, alongside features aimed at simplifying the hosting process (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 11:45 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Global hospitality platform Airbnb is looking to deepen its presence in India by expanding beyond traditional holiday destinations, strengthening the homestay ecosystem and bringing more local entrepreneurs onto its platform to tap the country's growing domestic travel market. In an interview with PTI, Airbnb India Country Manager Amanpreet Bajaj said the company's India growth strategy will focus on expanding quality accommodation supply, enabling more communities to participate in tourism and diversifying its offerings beyond stays through experiences and services. "We will also continue expanding quality supply, both in traditional leisure markets and metros and in emerging destinations such as spiritual corridors and nature-led locations. We want travellers to have more choices and local communities to benefit from tourism," Bajaj shared.

He highlighted that India is one of Airbnb's fastest-growing origin markets globally, with domestic travel emerging as a major growth driver. Over 85 per cent of bookings by Indian guests in the first half of 2026 were domestic, while almost 70 per cent of first-time bookers during the period were from Gen Z. The company is looking to expand its reach beyond established leisure destinations such as Goa and hill stations, with growing interest in cultural, spiritual, nature-led and rural tourism. Also Read

Juniper Hotels Q2FY27 net profit more than doubles to ₹37.2 crore

Chalet Hotels Q2 net profit rises 40% to ₹216 crore, revenue falls 32%

"We have a presence across India, and the travel map is widening as travellers look beyond traditional tourism hubs for nature, culture, heritage and local experiences," Bajaj said.

Destinations such as Kangra, East Khasi Hills and Srinagar, along with hill stations in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, are attracting attention, while Varanasi and Amritsar are emerging as important cultural and spiritual tourism destinations, he added. As demand spreads to newer locations, Airbnb is also focusing on developing accommodation supply and building a stronger host ecosystem in these markets. Its two-year memorandum of understanding with the Ministry of Tourism is aimed at strengthening India's homestay ecosystem through host training, digital onboarding and destination promotion. The company also conducts community meet-ups and training programmes to encourage more people to participate in tourism. It has piloted the Airbnb Entrepreneurship Academy in Goa to help prospective homestay hosts learn hospitality best practices and prepare to welcome guests.

Bajaj cited the company's long-standing partnership with the Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA) in rural Gujarat, under which women have received training to open their homes to visitors. He stressed that the economic benefits extend beyond the accommodation business. "Hosts have also told us that welcoming visitors creates opportunities beyond the home: local young people can provide transport, artisans can sell their products, and shops and restaurants can benefit. That is the multiplier effect of tourism on a local economy," Bajaj said. He shared that Airbnb will keep strengthening its core stays business while expanding what guests can do through experiences and services. Technology-led initiatives are another part of the strategy, with the company introducing AI-powered tools for searching, filtering and comparing homes, alongside features aimed at simplifying the hosting process.

Airbnb has introduced more than 250 product enhancements for hosts over recent years, including tools for listing homes, pricing guidance, AI-powered photo tours and an interactive earnings dashboard. The company wants to make hosting simpler while improving the quality and choice of accommodation available to travellers, Bajaj said. "The goal is not simply to capture more demand, but to meet the evolving needs of a new generation of Indian travellers, with Airbnb options across different price points, places and travel occasions," he observed.

item.title: Aluminium product makers seek zero import duty on raw metal ahead of Budget
item.description: Manufacturers' body ALEMAI has written a letter to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, seeking to bring down the basic customs duty on primary aluminium to zero ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Aluminium product makers seek zero import duty on raw metal ahead of Budget

Aluminium product makers seek zero import duty on raw metal ahead of Budget Manufacturers' body ALEMAI has written a letter to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, seeking to bring down the basic customs duty on primary aluminium to zero

The impact is particularly significant for MSMEs, for whom raw material prices constitute a substantial proportion of overall manufacturing costs | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 11:17 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Ahead of the Union budget for 2027-28, aluminium product manufacturers have urged the government to allow duty-free imports of raw metal to boost domestic consumption and enhance the competitiveness of small enterprises. Manufacturers' body ALEMAI has written a letter to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, seeking to bring down the basic customs duty on primary aluminium to zero, arguing that the current 7.5 per cent levy, which translates into an effective import duty of 8.25 per cent including social welfare surcharge, is hurting MSMEs (micro, small and medium enterprises) and domestic value addition. "We respectfully request the government in the forthcoming Union Budget...the basic customs duty on primary aluminium under tariff heading 7601 (be reduced) from 7.5 per cent to 0 per cent," Aluminium Extrusion Manufacturers Association of India (ALEMAI) said in the letter.   The measure, it said, can help strengthen the competitiveness of the country's downstream manufacturing ecosystem, encourage greater domestic value addition, support MSMEs, improve export competitiveness, and expand aluminium consumption across the economy. India has established a globally competitive primary aluminium industry and has significant potential to expand domestic aluminium consumption. However, the downstream aluminium sector, comprising a large number of MSMEs, continues to face a structural cost disadvantage due to the prevailing tariff structure on primary aluminium, the principal raw material, it said. Also Read

Hind Copper, SAIL, NMDC among 6 stocks on analysts radar amid metals slide

DGTR initiates anti-dumping probe into aluminium extrusion imports premium

Hindalco flags coal supply constraints, sees 5% rise in aluminium costs premium

CBAM: Let's get ready premium

Domestic demand for non-ferrous metals set to rise 8-9% in FY27 premium

Domestic primary aluminium prices are influenced by international prices and import-parity considerations. The customs duty applicable to imported primary aluminium consequently forms an important component of the domestic price benchmark, it said, adding that the issue has also been recognised by the Ministry of Mines in its Vision Document on Aluminium Sector 2025. The document estimates that in 2022, India's downstream sector paid approximately USD 470 million more than necessary to domestic primary aluminium producers on account of import-parity pricing. The document notes that this additional expenditure came at the expense of the downstream sector's growth and investment. The impact is particularly significant for MSMEs, for whom raw material prices constitute a substantial proportion of overall manufacturing costs. Higher input costs directly affect margins, capacity utilisation, investment decisions and the ability of Indian manufacturers to compete in both domestic and international markets. Besides, downstream manufacturers increasingly face competition from finished and semi-finished products imported at preferential or zero-duty rates under India's free trade agreements. This creates an asymmetry and an inverted duty structure in which Indian manufacturers face higher input costs while competing against imported products that enter the country at lower or zero tariff rates. Rationalising the customs duty on primary aluminium would help address this structural disadvantage and enable greater value addition within India. The proposed measure would reduce the input cost burden on downstream aluminium manufacturers, improve the competitiveness of MSMEs in export markets, and strengthen domestic manufacturing and value addition, it said.
